title: The knit stitch
subtitle: The foundation of knitted fabric and its k-tbl variant.
excerpt: The knit stitch (abbreviated k) is the right-side facing stitch that produces the V columns of stocking stitch. This deep dive covers the English-style throw, the Continental pick, and knitting through the back loop.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 1 (1886). Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), pp. 10-20. Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870).

glossaryTerms.definition: The basic right-side stitch produced by inserting the needle through the front of the stitch from left to right, wrapping the yarn anticlockwise, and drawing a new loop through. Abbreviated k.
Fabric produced by knitting every right-side row and purling every wrong-side row. UK name for what US patterns call stockinette. Abbreviated st st.
Inserting the needle into the back rather than the front leg of the stitch, producing a twisted stitch. Abbreviated k1tbl or ktbl.

content.text: The
knit stitch
(abbreviated k) is the primary building block of knitted fabric. Every row of knit stitches on the right side produces the smooth V columns you see in
stocking stitch

(US: stockinette). Knitting every row on both sides produces garter stitch, with its characteristic ridged, reversible texture. The knit stitch is entirely beginner territory; the technique below covers English-style yarn throwing and notes the Continental pick as an equally valid alternative.
What you need
DK yarn cast on to 4 mm needles (20-30 stitches gives enough width to feel the rhythm)
The stitch, step by step
English style (yarn in right hand, throwing):
Hold the left needle with stitches in the left hand, working yarn controlled in the right.
Insert the right needle tip into the first stitch on the left needle, entering from left to right through the front loop.
Wrap the working yarn anticlockwise around the right needle tip.
Draw the right needle back through the stitch, pulling the new loop forward.
Slip the old stitch off the left needle. One knit stitch completed.

Continental style (yarn in left hand, picking): steps 1-5 are the same, but instead of wrapping the yarn with the right hand, you catch the strand held by the left index finger by hooking it with the right needle tip. The result is identical fabric at a faster pace for many knitters.
The k-tbl variant
To work
knit through the back loop

(k1tbl), insert the needle into the back leg of the stitch rather than the front. The stitch will look twisted in the finished fabric, sitting with a crossed base. Twisted stitches appear in textured patterns, in some cast-on methods (the German twisted cast-on uses this move), and in lace where a firm, narrow column is required alongside an eyelet.
Where you will see it

Every knitting pattern contains the abbreviation k. Stocking stitch, garter stitch, rib, cables, lace, and colourwork are all built from knit and purl stitches in varying combinations. The knit stitch is the vocabulary; everything else is grammar.

items.symptom: Stitch falls off the left needle before it is worked
items.cause: Left thumb not holding the stitches back, or needle too slippery
items.fix: Keep the left thumb pressed gently against the first stitch on the left needle as you work. Bamboo needles grip the yarn more than metal and help until the rhythm is established.

items.symptom: New stitch is very tight and hard to slide
items.cause: Knitting into the back of the stitch by accident, or casting on too tightly
items.fix: Check the entry point: the right needle should enter from the left side of the stitch, not the right. If the stitch is still tight, work with a needle one size larger until tension relaxes.

items.cause: Accidentally working the yarn over at the start of a row as a new stitch
items.fix: At the beginning of a right-side row, the working yarn should hang toward you (at the front) if the first stitch is a purl, or away from you (at the back) if the first stitch is a knit. Check before working the first stitch of every row.

items.symptom: Finished fabric has an irregular, knobbly texture
items.cause: Mixing English and Continental technique mid-row, or varying tension
items.fix: Pick one style and work a full practice swatch in that style only. Tension evens out with repetition.
